digest.top_line: Salvage RT ± ADT: RTOG 9601 OS HR 1.13 at pre-SRT PSA <0.7 vs 0.45 at >1.5 ng/mL, arguing against routine ADT with early SRT (2018 commentary).
digest.tldr: Planning-focused day, no new trial readouts. Prostate carries it: pre-SRT PSA gates ADT benefit (RTOG 9601), and 60 Gy/20 fx moderate hypofx holds non-inferior across CHHiP, PROFIT and NRG 0415. H&N PNI framework sets 60 Gy bed, 50-60 Gy elective CN pathways; a case report flags phrenic nerve palsy ~2 yr after 50 Gy/4 fx lung SABR.

studies.name: Unilateral diaphragmatic paralysis after lung SABR abutting phrenic nerve
studies.tldr: Max point dose 57.7 Gy (BED 335.14 Gy, α/β=3) near the left phrenic nerve after 50 Gy/4 fx SABR, followed by hemidiaphragm paralysis at ~2 yr.
details: 🔍 Single case report: woman in her 50s, metastatic sinonasal adenoid cystic carcinoma, 2 lung mets
🔍 SABR 50 Gy in 4 fractions, VMAT, 4D-CT sim, amplitude-based expiratory gating
🔍 Uniform 5 mm PTV, limited to 3 mm into the mediastinum for the LUL mass
📊 Max point dose to the approximate phrenic nerve region 57.7 Gy (BED 335.14 Gy, α/β=3)
📊 L hemidiaphragm elevation first visible on CT at 23 mo, ~2 mo before dyspnea
📊 Sniff test confirmed L hemidiaphragmatic paralysis. Dyspnea first attributed to known asthma
📊 Conservative mgmt (breathing exercises, ambulation) improved symptoms within 3 mo. No plication
📊 No local recurrence at 38 mo. Paralysis persists on imaging

details.text: 🔗 Central-tumor SABR trials cited in source: no neuropathy, phrenic nerve never contoured

subdetails: Mediastinum outside PTV: max dose capped at prescription
PTV/mediastinum overlap: capped at 110% of prescription
Volume >105% kept as small as possible, GTV dose not compromised
Authors do NOT advocate reducing target coverage for mediastinal-abutting tumors

details: ⚠️ Phrenic nerve not visible on CT; 57.7 Gy is a dose to an approximated location
⚠️ Radiation nerve injury is a diagnosis of exclusion; no confirmatory test exists
⚠️ Concurrent L vocal cord paresis attributed to H&N RT 14 yr earlier, a second prior-RT exposure

verdict.rationale: n=1 case report; a single approximated point dose cannot define phrenic tolerance, and authors note pts with higher nerve doses and no injury.
verdict.audience: Lung SABR targets abutting the mediastinum along the phrenic nerve course

studies.significance: This is about planning and surveillance, not a tolerance: the authors contour the mediastinum as a surrogate, cap dose outside the PTV at prescription and the overlap at 110%. CT elevation came ~2 mo before dyspnea, so reviewing the hemidiaphragm on routine surveillance scans is the transferable step. The case also supports adding phrenic injury to consent.
studies.monday_clinic: In a pt with prior SABR to a lung tumor abutting the mediastinum who presents with new dyspnea, this supports considering phrenic nerve injury and a sniff test; it does not support de-escalating dose or coverage for mediastinal-abutting targets.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Single-patient case report** from one institution, with a planning review by a radiation oncologist and a thoracic radiologist.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Woman in her 50s with **metastatic adenoid cystic carcinoma of the sinonasal tract**, 12 yr from diagnosis, with prior resection, adjuvant skull-base RT, a VATS wedge and multiple SRS courses. Growing lung mets were the only known active disease.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **50 Gy in 4 fractions** to 2 lung mets, VMAT, 4D-CT simulation, expiratory gating, daily CBCT. PTV 5 mm, **limited to 3 mm into the mediastinum** for the LUL lesion.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Max point dose to the approximate phrenic region **57.7 Gy (BED 335.14 Gy, α/β=3)**. CT elevation at **23 mo**, dyspnea ~2 mo later, sniff-test-confirmed paralysis. **No local recurrence at 38 mo.**

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Symptoms improved within **3 mo of conservative management**, no surgery. Paralysis persists radiographically; pt asymptomatic at last visit.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: RTOG 0813, the Indiana phase 2 and the Stanford dose-adapted phase 2 reported **no neuropathy**, but **none contoured the phrenic nerve**. Single-institution series describe dose-associated but inconsistent SA node and recurrent laryngeal injury.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents pts receiving lung SABR to tumors abutting the mediastinum along the phrenic course. Does not represent peripheral lung targets away from the mediastinum, or a validated nerve dose constraint.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Nerve position is **approximated** on CT, so the reported dose is uncertain. The injury is a **diagnosis of exclusion**, and the pt had prior H&N RT with another cranial nerve deficit.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The prior trials' zero rate reflects a toxicity that was **neither contoured nor sought**, so true incidence is unknown. The authors call for a **dose-response analysis** of mediastinal-abutting SABR and a rare-complication registry.

studies.interpretation:
The value of this report is not the dose number. A single estimated point maximum of 57.7 Gy to a nerve that cannot be seen on CT cannot anchor a constraint, and the authors concede that other pts have received more without injury. What the case does establish is that the phrenic nerve belongs on the list of mediastinal structures SABR can injure, alongside the vagus and recurrent laryngeal nerves and the sinoatrial node, where single-institution series already describe a dose-associated but inconsistent pattern. The vocal cord series the authors cite makes the point well: symptomatic pts sat inside the range of doses asymptomatic pts tolerated, which suggests dose is necessary but not sufficient and that anatomic or host factors carry part of the risk.

Set against the central-tumor trials that shaped current practice, the absence of neuropathy in RTOG 0813, the Indiana phase 2 and the Stanford dose-adapted trial is less reassuring than it first looks. None of them contoured the phrenic nerve, and diaphragm elevation is easy to miss on surveillance imaging or to blame on something else; in this pt, dyspnea was first read as asthma. A toxicity that is not contoured, not prospectively sought, and diagnosed only by exclusion has an unknown rate in those trials, not a zero rate. The authors' suspicion of underreporting is plausible for exactly that reason.

The latency matters for follow-up. Elevation appeared on CT at 23 months and symptoms followed roughly 2 months later, a window beyond the follow-up of many SABR toxicity reports but inside the surveillance imaging a radiation oncologist already orders. Looking at the hemidiaphragm on those scans costs nothing and is the most transferable recommendation in the paper.

The planning recommendations deserve a narrower read than the list suggests. Contouring the mediastinum as a surrogate, holding dose outside the PTV to prescription and capping the PTV overlap at 110% are reasonable hotspot hygiene, but they reflect one institution's convention rather than outcome data, and the authors explicitly decline to trade target coverage for nerve sparing. That is the right balance for a complication this rare in pts whose alternative is local progression. This pt had no local recurrence at 38 months, which is the outcome the plan was built to protect.

What would move practice is the dose-response analysis the authors call for: a cohort of mediastinal-abutting targets with the phrenic course contoured retrospectively and diaphragm position scored on serial CT. Until that exists, the defensible use of this report is consent language and surveillance attention, not a new constraint and not a reason to underdose the target.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: This is about planning and surveillance, not a tolerance: the authors contour the mediastinum as a surrogate, cap dose outside the PTV at prescription and the overlap at 110%. CT elevation came ~2 mo before dyspnea, so reviewing the hemidiaphragm on routine surveillance scans is the transferable step.

open_questions: Phrenic nerve dose-response for mediastinal-abutting lung SABR
True incidence of SABR phrenic injury given likely underreporting

studies.name: Radiotherapy treatment planning for testicular seminoma
studies.tldr: 20 Gy/10 fx AP-PA fields with T12 superior and acetabular inferior borders; stage II boost 10 Gy/5 fx (IIA) or 16 Gy/8 fx (IIB).
details: 🔍 Evidence-based planning review, clinical stage IA-IIB seminoma post radical inguinal orchiectomy
🔍 Surveillance preferred for compliant stage I pts; adjuvant RT reserved for the minority choosing treatment

details.text: 💊 Management options by setting (per review pathways)

rows: Stage I, no prior pelvic/scrotal surgery
Modified dog-leg 20 Gy/10 fx + 10 Gy/5 fx boost
Modified dog-leg 20 Gy/10 fx + 16 Gy/8 fx boost

subdetails: Superior T12: Paly mapping, 69 stage II pts, no positive nodes above L1
Superior T12: Bruns, 80 pts, no relapses in reduced volume, median f/u 7.1 years
Inferior acetabulum: German cohort, 87 pts, no pelvic relapses

details: 🔗 TE18: 20 Gy/10 fx not inferior to 30 Gy/15 fx; less lethargy, faster return to work
🔗 TE10: para-aortic vs dog-leg fields → less acute toxicity, faster sperm count recovery
⚠️ IMRT lowers marrow/bowel V75%/V100%, but AP-PA keeps kidney, liver, bowel Dmean lower
⚠️ Large trials used a T11 superior border; T12 rests on mapping plus cohort data
studies.significance: The T12 superior border rests on mapping of 69 stage II pts with no positive nodes above L1, plus 80 pts without relapse in the reduced volume at median 7.1 years. The vascular CTV recipe (IVC +1.2 cm, aorta +1.9 cm, PTV 0.5 cm, block edge 0.7 cm) ports directly to CT-based planning, though large trials still used T11.
studies.monday_clinic: In stage IIA/IIB seminoma planned for modified dog-leg RT, this supports a T12 superior and acetabular inferior border; it does not extend to pts with prior pelvic or scrotal surgery, where classic dog-leg fields covering iliac and inguinal nodes apply.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Evidence-based review with planning recommendations, **not an outcomes study**. Draws on MRC TE10 and TE18, nodal-mapping series and prospective cohorts.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Clinical **stage IA, IB, IS, IIA and IIB** testicular seminoma after radical inguinal orchiectomy. 85% present with stage I and 11% with stage II disease.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **20 Gy in 10 fractions** to para-aortic (stage I) or modified dog-leg (stage II) AP-PA fields, then a boost of **10 Gy/5 fx (IIA)** or **16 Gy/8 fx (IIB)**. Borders: superior at the **top of T12**, dog-leg inferior at the **top of the acetabulum**. Clamshell shield for the remaining testis; no scrotal or prophylactic mediastinal RT.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: With 20 Gy, grade 2 and 3 leukopenia are **2% and 0**, so weekly CBCs are unnecessary. Late risks: RR of second pancreatic (3.8), colon (1.9) and gastric (4.1) cancers, and a **twofold or greater** cardiovascular risk beyond 15 years.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: TE18 supports 20 Gy over 30 Gy, and TE10 supports para-aortic over dog-leg fields for stage I. Seven-field IMRT lowers high-dose volumes to marrow and bowel, but **AP-PA keeps kidney, liver and bowel Dmean lower**, which is why AP-PA stays standard.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents clinical stage I-IIB seminoma post orchiectomy planned for photon AP-PA RT. Does not represent pts with horseshoe kidney, IBD or prior RT, for whom chemotherapy is preferred.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The T12 superior border rests on mapping and an 80-pt cohort, while **large trials used T11**. Vascular CTV margins come from nodal-location studies, with no outcome comparison against bony-anatomy fields.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Shrinking the volume at both ends ties the review together, justified by second-malignancy and cardiac risk. The review does not show that the reductions change late toxicity, and renal artery dose may limit the cardiovascular gain from a T12 border.

studies.interpretation:
This review is worth reading less for any single recommendation than for its argument that the seminoma treatment volume can shrink at both ends without losing control. How well that argument holds up depends on which border you look at. The move of the superior border from T11 to T12 rests on two lines of evidence: a nodal mapping series of clinical stage II pts that found no positive nodes above L1, and the Bruns cohort with no relapses in the cranially reduced volume. Both are reassuring, but neither is a comparative test. The authors concede that the large trials, TE10 and TE18, were run with the superior border at T11. So a reader adopting T12 relies on mapping plus a modest cohort, not randomized evidence. The payoff the authors describe, lower kidney, stomach and bowel dose, is a dosimetric argument and not an observed drop in second cancers or cardiac events. They also point out that renal artery irradiation may drive the cardiovascular harm, which caps what a cranial reduction can achieve.

The inferior border argument for dog-leg fields stands on firmer clinical ground. The German prospective cohort placed the border at the top of the acetabulum, saw no pelvic relapses, and a European consensus group adopted the position. Still, a cohort with no events in a region is limited by its size. That series also gave no cone down, so its control data do not carry over cleanly to the boost-based approach recommended here for stage IIA and IIB.

The vascular-anatomy CTV recipe is where the review is most prescriptive and least tested. The vessel expansions come from mapping studies of where nodes sit, which is the right input for coverage probability. But nothing here compares vascular-based 3D-CRT with bony-anatomy fields on outcomes. Marginal misses with bony fields motivate the change, and the idea that vascular contouring closes them is inferred, not shown. The authors are candid that the added complexity has to be weighed, and they keep 2D bony-anatomy fields as a legitimate choice for stage II disease.

The modality discussion is equally candid. Seven-field IMRT lowers high-dose volumes in marrow and bowel, but opposed AP-PA fields give lower mean and median doses to kidneys, liver and bowel. In a disease whose main late harm is second malignancy in exactly those organs, the low-dose bath counts, and that reasoning still favors AP-PA for most pts. Protons are left as an open cost-effectiveness question, not endorsed.

The broader frame matters most. The review treats surveillance as preferred for compliant stage I pts and reserves adjuvant RT for a minority, with carboplatin preferred when follow-up is unlikely. Read today, the planning detail is still a usable technical reference. But the document dates to 2012, and its stage I and stage II treatment hierarchies should be checked against current guidelines before they are treated as settled. What it does not settle is whether any of the volume reductions change late toxicity in practice.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Field design is the read: T12 superior and acetabular inferior borders, a vascular CTV (IVC +1.2 cm, aorta +1.9 cm) and stage II kidney limits of D50% ≤8 Gy for the dog-leg phase and ≤2 Gy for the boost. The T12 border is backed by mapping and an 80-pt cohort; large trials used T11.

open_questions: Does vascular-anatomy 3D-CRT reduce late toxicity vs bony-anatomy fields?
Proton cost-effectiveness vs photon RT or BEP x3 in seminoma

studies.name: Perineural invasion and perineural tumor spread in head and neck cancer
studies.tldr: Graded RT framework for PNI/PNTS: tumor bed 60 Gy, elective cranial nerve pathways 50-60 Gy retrograde to skull base, gross PNTS 70 Gy.
details: 🔍 Narrative review with author recommendations; dose data described as limited and mostly empirically derived

Aggressive salivary cancers (ACC, SDC) with microscopic PNI

details: 📊 Definitive RT for gross PNTS in skin cancer: disease control 50% to 57%
📊 Unresectable or subtotally resected salivary (mainly ACC): definitive RT control 36% to 93%, photon or particle
⚠️ cSCC extensive PNI: RT 2-yr DSS 73% vs unirradiated DFS 40%; different endpoints, retrospective
⚠️ Oral cavity: PNI link to local failure contested; adjuvant RT for early-stage PNI-only disease unsettled
💊 Microscopic PNI alone in resected mucosal SCC: not an indication for concurrent systemic therapy

studies.significance: The underused rule is interconnections: anastomotic pathways such as V to VII should always be covered with PNTS or a positive margin along an adjacent named nerve, retrograde to the skull base. Oral cavity SCC is the stated exception, with no skull-base CN coverage absent gross named-nerve or CN involvement.
studies.monday_clinic: In resected head and neck SCC or salivary cancer with only focal intratumoral microscopic PNI, this supports tumor-bed-only volumes; it does not extend to ACC/SDC histology, named or >0.1 mm nerve involvement, or radiographic PNTS, where the authors cover elective cranial nerve pathways to the skull base.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Narrative review with author recommendations built on **6 representative clinical cases**, published contouring guidelines, failure patterns and **collective experience**. The authors call the dose data **limited and mostly empirically derived**.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **Dose painting** is recommended in anatomically complex cases. CN coverage runs **retrograde toward the skull base**; anterograde coverage only when symptoms, the operative report or imaging suggest spread. Proton therapy is cited for reducing intermediate and low dose to the temporal lobe at the skull base.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Platinum and cetuximab rest on landmark head and neck radiosensitizer trials, but the authors do not extend them to **microscopic PNI alone** in resected mucosal SCC. For high-risk salivary cancers, Radiation Therapy Oncology Group trial 1008 was testing cisplatin with postoperative RT; until it reports, support is retrospective only.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents mucosal SCC, cutaneous SCC and salivary malignancies of the head and neck with PNI or PNTS, resected or unresectable. Does not represent early oral cavity SCC with PNI as the only adverse feature, where adjuvant RT benefit is unsettled.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The cSCC benefit sets **2-yr DSS 73%** beside **DFS 40%**, two different endpoints. **PNI definitions were not standardized** across oral cavity series, and nerve-caliber cut points (0.1 or 1 mm) vary by series, so the tier a patient falls into depends on the pathology read.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Positions RT as the default after PNI in mucosal SCC, cSCC and salivary cancers, with volume and dose scaled to PNI extent. The authors report **no active clinical trials focused on PNI**; preclinical data suggest low-dose nerve irradiation suppresses invasion through reduced GDNF.

studies.interpretation:
This piece is best read as a structured statement of expert practice, not a synthesis of outcome data. Its contribution is a graded framework: tumor-bed-only volumes for focal intratumoral microscopic PNI, extension along the innervating cranial nerve for high-risk histology or nerve features, and therapeutic dose along nerves with gross spread. That gradient is anatomically sensible and matches the described direction of failure, centripetally toward the skull base. What it lacks is any comparative evidence that elective cranial nerve coverage improves nerve-pathway control over a generous tumor-bed volume. The authors say plainly that dose selection rests on limited, empirically derived data plus collective experience, and that no clinical trial focused on PNI was active when they wrote.

The outcome numbers that do appear should move confidence less than their placement suggests. The cutaneous SCC result, 2-year disease-specific survival of 73% with radiation in extensive PNI against disease-free survival of 40% in unirradiated patients, sets two different endpoints side by side within a retrospective subset. It supports the direction (extensive, not focal, PNI benefits) but cannot size the effect. The definitive-RT control ranges for gross PNTS in skin cancer (50% to 57%) and for unresectable ACC (36% to 93%) span photon and particle series with different selection, and the width of the ACC range is itself the message: these are not figures to quote to a patient as an expected result.

The framework is most likely to be wrong in its middle tier. Extensive PNI, nerve-caliber thresholds (0.1 or 1 mm depending on the series) and the number of involved foci are not standardized, and the authors acknowledge controversy over their independent effect. Because the decision to follow a nerve to the foramen ovale or the geniculate ganglion turns on exactly these features, two pathologists reading the same specimen could place a patient in different volume tiers. The toxicity cost follows from that read: cochlear dose, and near-certain hearing loss if CN VII is followed into the internal acoustic canal, or temporal lobe and optic apparatus dose along V1 and V2.

Two boundaries are worth carrying into practice. Oral cavity SCC is carved out: PNI there usually sits in small unnamed fibers, its link to local failure is contested, and the authors do not extend volumes to the skull base without gross named-nerve involvement. And microscopic PNI alone in resected mucosal SCC is not, in their read, an indication for concurrent systemic therapy, which keeps the platinum decision tied to the conventional high-risk features rather than to nerve invasion.

For salivary cancers the authors deferred the cisplatin question to the cooperative-group trial then running. The volume and dose recommendations themselves would be tested best by patterns-of-failure series that record which nerve segments were covered and at what dose, since the claimed benefit is specifically along the nerve pathway and a tumor-bed recurrence endpoint cannot show it.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Interconnections are the underused rule: anastomotic pathways such as V to VII should always be covered with PNTS or a positive margin along an adjacent named nerve, retrograde to the skull base. Oral cavity SCC is the stated exception, with no skull-base CN coverage absent gross named-nerve involvement.

open_questions: Does elective cranial nerve coverage improve nerve-pathway control over tumor bed alone?
Benefit of concurrent cisplatin with postoperative RT for high-risk salivary cancers
Role of adjuvant RT in early oral cavity SCC with PNI as sole risk factor

sites.intro: Two 2018 pieces: PSA-gated ADT with SRT and a practical guide to 60 Gy/20 fx; both predate SPPORT/RADICALS-HD and mature PACE data.

studies.name: Risk stratification to guide hormone therapy with salvage RT
studies.tldr: Pre-SRT PSA predicts ADT benefit: RTOG 9601 OS HR 1.13 at PSA <0.7 vs 0.45 at >1.5 ng/mL; argues against routine ADT with early SRT.
details: 🔍 Single-author Q&A commentary (Red Journal 2018); no new patient data

details.text: 📊 ADT benefit by pre-SRT PSA stratum, as cited in source

rows: GETUG-AFU-16 · crude biochemical control benefit (PSA <0.5 vs >0.5)

details: 📐 RTOG 9601: interaction test by pre-SRT PSA reported significant
📐 Higher Gleason score did not predict who benefits from added HT
⚠️ RTOG 9601 excluded PSA <0.5 for much of accrual; only ~10% had PSA ≤0.3
⚠️ GETUG-AFU-16 biochemical gain confounded: GnRH agonist keeps testosterone subnormal an additional 6-12 mo
🔗 RTOG 9408: 4 mo HT improved BCR by 10% even in low-risk intact prostate, near GETUG at PSA <0.5
🔗 ICECaP (>28,000 men on RCTs): BCR not a survival surrogate; DM correlation over 0.9
🔍 RT: 64 to 72 Gy judged sufficient for microscopic bed/pelvic disease at early SRT

details.text: 📊 Simplified ADT-with-SRT framework (source Table 3). *Discuss HT if minimal comorbidity, 12-yr life expectancy, multiple high-risk features

subdetails: PSA <0.7: NRG GU-006 (SRT ± apalutamide); excludes PSA >1.0
PSA ≥0.7, pN+, or pT3b-T4 / pattern 5: FORMULA-509 or RTOG 3506 (ADT both arms + second-gen HT)
Persistent PSA ≥0.2: NRG GU-002 (docetaxel question)

details: ⚠️ 2018 opinion; predates later salvage-ADT RCTs (SPPORT, RADICALS-HD) and PSMA PET restaging
studies.significance: Pre-SRT PSA, not Gleason, is the variable that predicted ADT benefit in RTOG 9601: OS HR 1.13 at PSA <0.7 vs 0.45 at >1.5 ng/mL. The GETUG-AFU-16 biochemical gain at PSA <0.5 (12%) sits near the 10% RTOG 9408 gave low-risk intact pts, so it reads as PSA suppression, not disease control.
studies.monday_clinic: In post-RP recurrence going to early SRT at PSA <0.7 ng/mL, this questions adding first-generation ADT outside a trial; it does not extend to PSA >1.5 ng/mL or GG 4-5 at higher PSA, where the framework adds STADT or LTADT.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Single-author **Q&A commentary**, no new patient data. Re-reads the two salvage RT ± HT randomised trials (**RTOG 9601**, **GETUG-AFU-16**) by pre-SRT PSA and proposes a simplified PSA × grade group framework.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Argues early SRT targets disease still confined to the prostate bed and/or pelvis, where microscopic disease is controlled with **64 to 72 Gy**. Above PSA 0.7 ng/mL, micrometastatic disease becomes more likely and systemic therapy is the stated need.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: RTOG 9601 is framed as mostly **late SRT** and GETUG-AFU-16 as mostly **early SRT**, with cutoffs of 0.7 and 0.5 ng/mL respectively. Benefit tracks PSA in both: RTOG 9601 OS HR **1.13 vs 0.45** (PSA <0.7 vs >1.5), GETUG crude biochemical benefit **12% vs 36%** (PSA <0.5 vs >0.5).

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents post-prostatectomy men with rising PSA weighing ADT alongside salvage RT. Does not represent persistent post-op PSA, pN+ disease, or men restaged with molecular imaging.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: PSA strata are subgroups of trials not powered for them, and the early vs late split pools two trials with different cutoffs and agents (bicalutamide vs 6 mo GnRH agonist). The ICECaP surrogacy data were unpublished when cited.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The strongest point is that biochemical control under a GnRH agonist measures suppressed PSA, not disease, so a GETUG BCR gain cannot justify ADT for early SRT. The framework **ignores tumor biology**, which the author flags as the open gap NRG GU-006 was built to test.

studies.interpretation:
The argument here depends on treating the two salvage-ADT randomised trials as studies of different disease states rather than as two attempts at the same question. RTOG 9601 excluded men with PSA below 0.5 ng/mL for a large part of its accrual, so it mostly tested ADT with late salvage RT. GETUG-AFU-16 mostly enrolled early salvage. Read that way, the trials do not conflict: the OS benefit in RTOG 9601 sits at higher PSA (HR 0.45 above 1.5 ng/mL) and disappears or reverses below 0.7 (HR 1.13), with a significant interaction, while Gleason score did not separate who benefits. The biology the author offers is coherent for an RT reader. After prostatectomy there is no gland making PSA, so a rising PSA tracks spread from bed to pelvic nodes to distant sites, and the lower the PSA at SRT, the more likely the field still covers all the disease.

The more persuasive half is the case against biochemical endpoints. A GnRH agonist keeps testosterone subnormal for months after the last dose, so any trial measuring time to PSA recurrence partly measures how long it suppressed PSA. The author's comparison is useful: GETUG's biochemical gain at PSA under 0.5 is about the same size as the 10% RTOG 9408 showed for low-risk intact prostate cancer, a population few would now give ADT to on that basis. Pairing that with ICECaP, where distant metastasis tracked survival and biochemical recurrence did not, sets the bar at a distant metastasis benefit. That bar is defensible, though the ICECaP surrogacy work was unpublished when this was written.

Confidence should be tempered in three places. The PSA strata are subgroups of trials not powered for them, and the source gives no confidence intervals around HR 1.13, so a harm signal at low PSA is not established. The early vs late construct pools trials with different cutoffs (0.7 vs 0.5) and different agents (bicalutamide vs a GnRH agonist), so the agent and the disease state are confounded. And the GETUG stratum figures are crude rates, not adjusted estimates.

The decision this moves is narrow and specific: whether to add first-generation ADT to early SRT at low PSA when the pt is not on a trial. It does not argue against ADT at high PSA, in node-positive disease, or with multiple adverse features; the framework escalates to short- and long-term ADT there. It also leaves the biology question open, which the author concedes, and points to biomarker-stratified trials as the way to settle it.

A reader in 2026 should treat this as a 2018 position. It predates the later salvage-ADT randomised data (SPPORT, RADICALS-HD) and routine PSMA PET restaging, both of which bear on where the PSA thresholds should sit. Its durable contribution is the endpoint logic, not the exact cutoffs.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Pre-SRT PSA, not Gleason, predicted ADT benefit in RTOG 9601 (OS HR 1.13 at PSA <0.7 vs 0.45 at >1.5 ng/mL). At low PSA the 64 to 72 Gy field likely covers the disease, and the GETUG biochemical gain reads as testosterone suppression rather than control.

open_questions: Does a genomic classifier identify early-SRT pts who benefit from ADT?
Does second-generation AR inhibition add to SRT at low PSA?
Do PSMA PET restaging shift the PSA thresholds for adding ADT?

studies.name: Moderate hypofractionation for prostate cancer: a user's guide
studies.tldr: 2018 practical review: CHHiP, PROFIT and NRG 0415 all non-inferior at 5-6 yr; 60 Gy/20 fx preferred, with planning aims and patient-selection caveats.

details.text: 📊 The three large non-inferiority RCTs, as summarized in review text

details: 📊 5-yr biochemical-clinical failure-free survival in the order of 85% to 90% across all three trials
📊 Late G≥3 toxicity 1%–4% across the three trials, regardless of schedule

NRG 0415: small increase in late G2 GI and GU with hypofractionation
NRG 0415 hypo arm carried higher BED (128 vs 118 Gy, α/β 3)
CHHiP: no difference in late effects on clinician- or patient-reported measures

details.text: 📊 Princess Margaret phase 2, 60 Gy/20, >10 yr f/u: any G3 toxicity 2%
subdetails: Late ≥G2 GI: 4% at 5 yr, unchanged at 8 yr
Late ≥G2 GU: 9% at 5 yr, 12% at 8 yr

Margins down to 3 to 5 mm with continuous intrafraction monitoring

⚠️ 2018 snapshot: HYPO-RT-PC cited as preliminary abstract only, PACE still ongoing at writing
studies.significance: Most relative contraindications fall away on this evidence: the IPSS >12 GU signal is a post hoc FCCC subgroup unconfirmed in larger trials, 8% of CHHiP pts had prior TURP, and no trial excluded on gland size. The planning layer transfers directly: ~7 mm CTV-PTV margin with daily IGRT and whole-organ OAR contours.
studies.monday_clinic: In localized intermediate-risk prostate cancer treated to the prostate ± proximal SV, this supports 60 Gy/20 fx over conventional schedules; it does not extend to elective pelvic nodal RT or to the Gleason ≥9 very-high-risk men CHHiP excluded.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Brief practical review of moderate hypofractionation evidence (seven randomised trials reported to date), anchored on **CHHiP, PROFIT and NRG Oncology 0415**, plus author-developed planning aims.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Trial cohorts had median age 67, 69 and 71 yr (NRG 0415, CHHiP, PROFIT) and WHO 0-1 performance status. **Intermediate-risk** disease carries the strongest evidence; CHHiP's 12% high-risk excluded Gleason ≥9.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **60 Gy in 20 fractions** preferred, delivered over ~4 weeks (median 29 days in CHHiP). IMRT/VMAT with daily IGRT, **~7 mm CTV-PTV margin**, 3 to 5 mm with intrafraction monitoring.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Late G≥3 toxicity **1%–4%** across the three trials. A small increase in temporary acute GI toxicity with the short-course schedules.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: HYPRO's 64.6 Gy/19 arm was **dose-escalated** (EQD2 90 Gy, α/β 1.5), so its toxicity is not a test of equivalent hypofractionation. The NRG 0415 GI/GU increase likewise tracks a higher BED (128 vs 118 Gy).

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents localized prostate cancer, intermediate-risk dominant, treated to prostate ± SV with IMRT and daily IGRT. Does not represent elective pelvic nodal RT or very-high-risk disease (Gleason ≥9) excluded from CHHiP.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Late GU toxicity can still rise beyond 5 yr (PMH cohort ≥G2 GU 9% at 5 yr, 12% at 8 yr). Extreme hypofractionation was only preliminary at writing, so the review predates mature SBRT data.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Consistency across three heterogeneous comparators and ADT policies is the main reassurance. The authors argue technique and selection now matter more than **modest differences in dose-fractionation**.

studies.interpretation:
This guide argues less about whether moderate hypofractionation works, since the three non-inferiority trials had largely settled that by 2018, and more about where the evidence stops. That boundary is the useful part for an RT reader. CHHiP, PROFIT and NRG Oncology 0415 each used a different conventional comparator (74 Gy, 78 Gy and 73.8 Gy) and a different ADT policy, yet all three landed with hazard ratios below 1.0. Agreement across that much design heterogeneity is stronger reassurance than any one trial's interval, which matters because the upper bounds (1.2 in PROFIT, 1.14 in NRG 0415) leave room a skeptic would point to.

The weakest plank is follow-up, with medians of 5.2, 5.8 and 6 years. The authors lean on two arguments. The first is that dose-escalation trials produced biochemical gains that never became survival differences, so a late efficacy divergence is unlikely. The second is the Princess Margaret phase 2 cohort at 60 Gy/20 with more than 10 years of follow-up. That cohort reassures more on control than on toxicity: GU ≥G2 rose from 9% at 5 years to 12% at 8 years, which is exactly the late drift the randomised data cannot yet exclude. The authors note many events were transient, but cumulative incidence is the number a reader quoting risk should keep in mind.

The HYPRO contrast is instructive. Its 64.6 Gy/19 arm was a dose-escalation design (EQD2 90 Gy at α/β 1.5), and its toxicity penalty reads as a dose problem rather than a fractionation problem. The same logic covers the NRG 0415 GI/GU increase, where the hypofractionated arm carried a higher BED (128 vs 118 Gy). The practical lesson is that 60 Gy/20 is not interchangeable with any schedule that merely uses fewer fractions; the evidence attaches to a specific biologic dose.

On patient selection the review is permissive, and mostly with reason. The IPSS >12 signal from Fox Chase was a post hoc subgroup that larger trials have not reproduced, and neither prior TURP nor gland size excluded pts from the big trials. The thinner ground is anticoagulation: CHHiP excluded it, and the Arcangeli haematuria signal tracked bladder dose, so in that subgroup planning quality carries more of the safety argument than the trial data do. The point that CHHiP GI toxicity ran around 50% lower than in RT01 supports the authors' broader claim that technique outweighs fractionation.

Two gaps carry forward into practice. No large hypofractionation trial treated elective nodes, so the result says nothing about pelvic nodal fields. CHHiP excluded the very-high-risk end, so high-risk extrapolation rests on almost 400 men given short-course ADT. Finally, this is a 2018 snapshot: HYPO-RT-PC and PACE appear only as preliminary or ongoing, so its framing of moderate schedules as the settled answer should be read against the extreme-hypofractionation data that have matured since.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Most relative contraindications fall away on this evidence: the IPSS >12 GU signal is a post hoc FCCC subgroup unconfirmed in larger trials, 8% of CHHiP pts had prior TURP, and no trial excluded on gland size. The planning layer transfers directly: ~7 mm CTV-PTV margin with daily IGRT and whole-organ OAR contours.

Extreme hypofractionation vs moderate schedules long-term
Late GU toxicity trajectory beyond 10 years

papers.journal: Journal of Medical Imaging and Radiation Oncology
papers.abstract: Summary Three large randomised controlled trials have been published in the last year demonstrating the non‐inferiority of moderate hypofractionation compared to conventional fractionation for localised prostate cancer with respect to both disease control and late toxicity at 5 years. Furthermore, no clinically significant differences in patient‐reported outcomes have emerged. More mature follow‐up data are now also available from phase 2 studies confirming that moderate hypofractionation is associated with low rates of significant toxicity at 10 years. Moving forward it is likely that appropriate patient selection, integration of androgen deprivation and attention to optimising technique will play a more important role than modest differences in dose‐fractionation schedules. Here we briefly review the evidence, discuss issues of patient selection and provide an approach to implementing moderately hypofractionated radiation therapy for prostate cancer in clinical practice.
